sections.history: Thirunavaya, in Malappuram district, lies on the north bank of the Bharathapuzha, and its temple is the Divya Desam called Thirunavai in the Alvar hymns. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvar saints in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and belongs to Malai Nadu, the Kerala country. Nammalvar is counted among its singers, and one source adds Thirumangai Alvar. The presiding Lord is Navamukunda, and the Goddess Malarmangai Nachiyar has a separate sreekovil of her own, an arrangement uncommon among the Vishnu temples of Kerala. The riverbank by the temple was the ground of the Mamankam, a medieval festival held every twelve years that carried great political significance in the days of the Zamorins.
sections.architecture: The temple stands by the north bank of the Bharathapuzha, and the river is central to its setting; the sanctum of Navamukunda looks out over a precinct that opens to the water’s edge. A distinguishing feature is the separate sreekovil for the Goddess Malarmangai Nachiyar, rare among the Kerala Vishnu temples, where the consort more often shares the Lord’s sanctum. The names of its vimana and tank are not firmly recorded, so none is given here.
sections.legends: The memory of the Mamankam hangs over the place. This great festival of the Bharathapuzha was held every twelve years on the river bank beside the temple, gathering merchants, rulers and pilgrims in the medieval centuries, and is remembered in the Zamorin era as an event of high political importance. Devotionally, the shrine’s legend is its Alvar tradition: the praise of Nammalvar and Thirumangai Alvar that makes it a Divya Desam, sung of the Lord Navamukunda on the banks of the river.
sections.festivals: Beyond the memory of the Mamankam, Thirunavaya is best known for Karkidaka Vavu, the new-moon day of the month of Karkidakam, when devotees perform bali tarpanam, ancestral rites, on the river bank; pilgrims come from across northern Kerala. Vaikunta Ekadashi is also observed as at other Vaishnava shrines. Dates follow the calendar of the month and the temple, so confirm locally.
sections.experience: Come for the quiet of the Bharathapuzha bank and for the pairing of two shrines, the Lord Navamukunda and the Goddess in her own sreekovil, which is rare in Kerala. Take time to walk to the river and to recall the Mamankam on its ground. Those who offer ancestral rites on Karkidaka Vavu should expect large crowds and follow the guidance of the priests.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions, usually with a midday closure; festival days are busiest. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thirunavaya is in Malappuram district on the north bank of the Bharathapuzha. It has its own railway station on the Shoranur–Kozhikode line, and Tirur and Kuttippuram are nearby towns with road links; autorickshaws and taxis serve the short distances. The nearest airport is Kozhikode. Expect heavy crowds on Karkidaka Vavu.
